1:
Psalm 16 wears a golden title, and the witnesses linger over the single word “Michtam” before the prayer is read. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry translates it a golden psalm, a very precious one, more to be valued than much fine gold, because it speaks so plainly of Christ and his resurrection, the true treasure hidden in the field of the Old Testament. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke canvasses the ancient guesses — the Chaldee’s “a straight sculpture of David,” the Septuagint’s “inscription on a pillar,” as though the psalm were engraved to keep it in remembrance — and, deriving michtam from a root meaning pure or stamped gold, allows the sense of a golden psalm worthy to be written in letters of gold, like the golden verses of Pythagoras; yet he confesses his doubts of all such title-meanings. The reformed John Calvin weighs the same two views, that the word marks a poem fit to be written in gold or engraved on a durable pillar for everlasting remembrance, but inclines rather to take it for some kind of tune or melody, the words in the psalm-titles being often old airs.

Then the prayer opens, “Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust,” and the schools read it as the voice of Christ. The reformed John Gill notes that prayer is proper to Christ as man, who offered supplications to his God, the word here rendered God being the strong and mighty God, with whom all things are possible; the petition was heard, Christ being preserved from Herod’s rage, sustained in the wilderness, and kept through his ministry till his hour was come. Clarke reads it as the prayer of the man Christ Jesus entering his atoning work, especially the passion in Gethsemane, where it was the manhood, not the Godhead, that suffered, and where the very name El, the strong God, is exactly suited to a frail humanity about to bear the load due the whole race. The latin-fathers Augustine hears the King speaking in the character of the human nature He assumed, whose royal title was set forth at his passion; and the puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon takes “preserve me” as “guard me,” even as bodyguards surround their monarch, so that the manhood of Jesus needed preserving and the elect were preserved in his preservation, the cry an anticipation of the intercession of John 17. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause “for I have found refuge in thee” (as in Ps. 7:1), the verb a preterite; while Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, judge from the compressed and antiquated language that David may be inferred as the author, a friend of God in danger of death yet with no trace of gloomy struggle in the whole song.
2:
The dedication that follows is spoken, on the received text, by the soul to its Lord, “O my soul, thou hast said unto the LORD, Thou art my Lord.” The reformed John Gill takes it for an apostrophe of Christ to his own soul, the supplied words “O my soul” being warranted by the Targum and by Jarchi, Aben Ezra, and Kimchi. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads “Thou art my Lord” as Adonai, my prop, stay, or support, the Messiah deriving his being and support from Jehovah, without which the man Christ could not have sustained his sufferings nor made atonement for the world. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon hears the Lord Jesus vowing allegiance before the throne of Jehovah for our sakes, and bids us be like him when our soul, in the presence of the heart-searching God, declares its full consent to his rule, “Thou art my Lord.”

Over the next clause, “my goodness extendeth not to thee,” the witnesses divide, and Ellicott warns that the whole passage is exceedingly corrupt. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the humbler devotional sense: Clarke renders “my bounty is not to thee,” for what the Messiah does can add nothing to the divinity, though it extends to the saints and the excellent ones; John Wesley glosses it simply, “thou dost not need me or my service, nor art capable of any advantage from it.” Spurgeon presses the same, that the work of redemption was not needful on account of any necessity in the Divine Being, who would have been inconceivably glorious had the whole race perished and no atonement been offered. But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott mounts a textual case against this reading. The ancient versions favour “I said” over “thou hast said” (the italicised “O my soul” being a mere gloss from the Chaldee), yielding the plain “I said to Jehovah, Thou art my Lord, I have no good besides thee.” The Authorized Version’s “extendeth,” he grants, introduces the fine thought that merit lives from man to man and not from man to God; but that could not have been the original sense, since “my good,” as the verses on the portion and the cup will show, means happiness, not conduct. So the division is genuine: whether the line confesses that a man’s goodness adds nothing to God, as the Wesleyan and Puritan voices hear it, or declares, with Ellicott, that the poet has no good, no happiness, apart from God himself.
3:
From God the psalm turns to God’s people, and the witnesses gather on the saints “that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight.” The reformed John Gill unfolds who they are: set apart by the Father in election, their sins expiated by the blood of Christ, sanctified by the Spirit, and living a holy conversation; and he asks why they are called saints “in the earth” — not to part them from the saints in heaven, to whom the goodness of Christ equally reaches, but, as Aben Ezra observes, from the angels who are also called saints, or simply to mark the place of their abode, scattered up and down the earth, reached by the kindness of Christ despite all their meanness and imperfection in themselves. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry calls them the excellent ones, great and magnificent, yet some so poor that they need David’s goodness extended to them; God makes them excellent by his grace, so that the righteous is more excellent than his neighbour, and they are his jewels, his peculiar treasure, in whom all who have taken the Lord for their God delight because they bear his image.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the two Hebrew words: the “excellent” are the addirey, the noble or supereminent ones who through faith and patience inherit the promises, and the “saints” the kedoshim, the consecrated, perhaps the first planters of Christianity, the evangelists and apostles separated to preach among the Gentiles, in whom was all the delight of Christ. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, emending the awkward Hebrew, reads a single flowing sentence, “and of the saints who are in the earth, they are the excellent in whom is all my delight”; and the latin-fathers Augustine hears “the saints who are on His earth” as the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose hope is fixed by an anchor in that country, though they are as yet conversant in the flesh.

Here one voice strikes a dissenting note on the psalm’s reference. Reading the verse of a singular respect and love borne to all saints for God’s sake, whose friends and servants they are and whose image they bear, the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley judges that this “more properly agrees to David than to Christ, whose goodness was principally designed for, and imparted to, sinners.” Where the other witnesses press the verse toward the delight of Christ in his people, Wesley marks it as one place that fits the type, David, better than the antitype — an early sounding of the David-and-Messiah question that will divide them more sharply at the psalm’s close.
4:
A dark counter-image now falls across the psalm, the multiplied sorrows of the idolater, “their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god.” The reformed John Gill refers the sorrows to the idolaters themselves, not, as Aben Ezra would have it, to the saints grieved by their idolatry. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the doom of those mad upon their idols, pursuing them as eagerly as if they feared they would escape: those that multiply gods multiply griefs to themselves, for whoever thinks one God too little will find two too many, and yet hundreds not enough. Their drink-offerings of blood he abhors, for at God’s altar the drinking of blood was strictly forbidden, the atoning blood being holy, whereas the devil prescribed his worshippers to drink it and so learn cruelty. Some, Henry adds, apply the verse to Christ himself, whose offered sacrifice was not the blood of bulls and goats, which he never so much as named, but his own blood.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that the Hebrew has no word for God, so that “another” may as well be another Messiah, the whole falling upon the unbelieving Jews who would not have the true Christ and whose sorrows have been multiplied for more than eighteen centuries; and he explains that a “drink-offering of blood” is properly the libation poured on the blood of a sacrifice already made, all such offerings ceasing under the Christian dispensation now that Christ has offered himself. John Wesley keeps the plainer sense of Gentile idol-worship, in which the heathen sometimes drank part of the blood of their sacrifices, and whose very names David will not take upon his lips.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses great variation among the ancient versions, and, with a few changes of pointing, reads “they shall multiply their sorrows who change to another god.” Behind the verb rendered “hasten,” which can mean to buy a wife, he detects the common prophetic figure of idolatry as adultery and an allusion to the curse on Eve in Genesis 3:16; the “libations of blood” he refers to the ghastly rites of Moloch and Chemosh, and the refusal to name the idols to the Hebrew horror of even pronouncing a false god’s name, baal being replaced by bosheth, the shameful thing; for the refusal to take their names on the lips he compares the command of Exodus 23:13, that the name of other gods be not so much as heard from an Israelite’s mouth. So the witnesses part chiefly over the target: whether David warns against literal idolaters and their bloody altars, as Gill, Henry, Wesley, and Ellicott take it, or whether, with Clarke, the prophecy reaches past them to the unbelieving nation still hastening after another Messiah.
5:
“The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot” — and the witnesses hear the choice of a soul that wants no other happiness. The reformed John Gill takes the words as spoken by Christ the priest, in allusion to the Levitical priests, who had no inheritance in Canaan but the Lord himself for their portion; they express the strong love and satisfaction Christ found in God, in whom his goodness and happiness as man lay. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise makes the Messiah the speaker: Jehovah is his portion, and it is God who has given him this lot — to redeem mankind, to receive from his hand the cup of suffering that he might impart the cup of consolation, and has instituted the cup of blessing to commemorate that passion and death. John Wesley reads a plainer contentment, “I rejoice in God as my portion, and desire no better,” the cup being the portion put into it as at ancient feasts, where each guest had his measure of meat and wine allotted him.

The grammatical-historical witnesses ground the imagery in the law and the land. Charles Ellicott points to the Levitical portion of Numbers 18:20, “I am thy portion and thine inheritance,” and imagines the poet exiled from his actual inheritance in Canaan consoling himself with the better part that cannot be taken away, quoting Savonarola’s saying, “What must not he possess who possesses the possessor of all!” and Paul’s word that all things are ours because we are Christ’s and Christ is God’s; the cup, as in Ps. 11:6, had already become a synonym for one’s condition in life. Keil and Delitzsch add that the measuring lines are cast and fall to a man just where his property is assigned him (Micah 2:5; Josh. 17:5), so that the pleasurable fellowship of God has become his paradisaic possession. On the closing clause, “thou maintainest my lot,” Ellicott marks a peculiar Hebrew verb: God does not merely dispose the lot, as he does even for unbelievers, but holds it fast in his hand; and he reports Hitzig’s plausible conjecture, tomid for tomikh, which would yield “thou art ever my lot.” The witnesses do not quarrel over the contentment; they differ only over the speaker — whether the exiled David or the Messiah who takes God for his portion — and over the single disputed word that binds the lot to God’s keeping hand.
6:
The choice becomes a song of contentment, “the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.” The reformed John Gill reads the lines, by which land was measured and apportioned, of the church and people given to Christ as his portion, and so takes the sense to be pleasant persons rather than pleasant places — the elect as Christ saw them in his Father’s decrees, clothed in his righteousness and washed in his blood, a bride adorned for him in the New Jerusalem; though he allows that Aben Ezra and Kimchi supply the word “places,” and that Christ delighted even in the very spots where he knew his people would dwell. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the Messianic key: “I have got a rich inheritance of immortal spirits,” a Church, an innumerable multitude of saints who shall dwell with him for ever, while he himself, as man, shall have a name above every name and be raised to the throne. John Wesley reads the pleasant places of a land flowing with milk and honey, and above all blessed with the presence and knowledge of God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains only the figure: the measuring cords are said to “fall” because, after the measuring, the portions were distributed by lot (Josh. 17:5; Micah 2:5). The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon lets the verse open into the joy of the Redeemer: Jesus found the way of obedience to lead into pleasant places, and could say, “Lo, I come; I delight to do thy will, O my God”; no man was ever so acquainted with grief, yet none ever tasted such joy in service, the joy set before him sending its beams down the rugged places where he endured the cross. He was well content with the blood-bought portion the lines of electing love had marked off as his own, and asks no goodlier heritage than that his beloved be with him where he is; and all the saints, Spurgeon adds, may use the same grateful language, discontented spirits being as unlike Jesus as the croaking raven is unlike the cooing dove. Our Lord was poorer than we are, Spurgeon observes, having nowhere to lay his head, yet he never murmured, and martyrs after him have been happy even in dungeons. The witnesses do not divide over the gladness; only Gill turns the pleasant places from ground to people, hearing in the goodly heritage the saints themselves in whom the portion of Christ lies.
7:
Contentment turns to thanks and self-examination, “I will bless the LORD, who hath given me counsel: my reins also instruct me in the night seasons.” The reformed John Gill notes that thanksgiving, like prayer, belongs to Christ as man and Mediator, who here determines to praise God for counsel and instruction. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the counsel as given by God’s word and Spirit, while the psalmist’s own reins — his conscience, called the reins in Jer. 17:10 — instructed and admonished him in the night-season, when he was silent and retired, catechizing him and quickening him to live as one who had God for his portion.

The wesleyan-arminian voices hold the Messianic and the devotional together. Adam Clarke observes that Jesus as man received all his wisdom from God (Luke 2:40-52), and that the reins or kidneys, hidden deep in the body, stand for the most secret workings of the soul, which are to be devoted wholly to God, the kidneys and their fat being always burnt in sacrifice to signify it; the “night seasons” he reads of the time of the passion, when Christ’s secret purposes concerning man’s redemption upheld him, for the joy set before him he endured the cross (Heb. 12:2). John Wesley has God inspire the very wisdom by which the psalmist chose the Lord for his portion, the reins being his inward thoughts and affections moved by the Holy Spirit, and the night the season when, others sleeping, his mind was working upon God in holy meditation.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the two verbs: “given me counsel” means led to a right and happy choice of the way of life, and “instruct me” is better “warn me,” since conscience echoes the voice of God, the Hebrew word carrying from its root the sense of a binding obligation, so that once the divine monition is heard it becomes a law to the good man, warning him of the least deviation. Keil and Delitzsch see the whole closing strophe rising here like seven rays of light toward the blessed prospect that has no need to fear death. The witnesses do not divide; whether they hear the man Christ instructed by his Father in the night of his passion, or the believer catechized by his own conscience in the night of his meditation, all read the verse as the grateful acknowledgment that the wise and happy choice of God for a portion is itself the gift of God.
8:
Here the psalm reaches the words Peter took up at Pentecost, “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved,” and with them the witnesses face the question that governs the whole song — how much is David’s and how much is Christ’s. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry answers plainly: all these verses are quoted by Peter (Acts 2:25-28), who tells us expressly that David speaks of Christ and of his resurrection; the “I shall not be moved” implies that Christ should be struck at, as in his agony, yet three things bore him up — the respect he had to his Father’s will, the assurance of his Father’s presence at his right hand (an angel strengthening him, Luke 22:43), and the prospect of a glorious issue, for the joy set before him he endured the cross (Heb. 12:2). The reformed John Gill takes “I have set the Lord always before me” not of the fear of God or the law, as Jarchi would have it, but of the Lord himself, on whom Christ kept his eye through his whole life, aiming always at his Father’s glory. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that the passage is applied by Peter to the death and resurrection of Christ, who as man had the constant presence, approbation, and support of God at his right hand, so that nothing could swerve him from fulfilling the divine counsel.

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon dwells on the fear of death that cast its shadow over the Redeemer, who “was heard in that he feared,” till hope shone full upon his soul and, with a continued eye to Jehovah, he surveyed the future in holy confidence; the apostle’s version, “I foresaw the Lord always before my face” (Acts 2:25), shows that the eye of Jesus’ faith discerned beforehand the continuance of divine support. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lets a plainer image stand: “at my right hand” is military, the shield of the right-hand comrade a protection to the man beside him (Ps. 121:5).

It is John Wesley who marks the pivot most exactly. Hitherto, the wesleyan-arminian Wesley says, David seems to have spoken with respect to himself, presenting God to his mind as witness and judge; but now he is “transported by the spirit of prophecy, and carried above himself, to speak as a type of Christ,” in whom this and the following verses were truly accomplished. So the witnesses divide not over the fact that Christ is meant but over the seam: where Henry, Gill, and Clarke find Christ throughout, and Keil and Delitzsch hear a real David whose confidence the promise fulfils, Wesley locates the exact verse at which David’s own voice is caught up beyond itself into prophecy.
9:
The confidence overflows into joy of heart, tongue, and body, “therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoiceth: my flesh also shall rest in hope.” The reformed John Gill reads “my heart is glad” of an inward joy and fulness, the same, he says, as rejoicing in spirit, because of the presence of the Lord. Over “my glory” the witnesses part. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it for the tongue, so called because bestowed on us to glorify God (Ps. 57:8) and quoted as such by Peter (Acts 2:26), though he grants that “soul bids as fair” for the meaning; John Wesley likewise makes it the tongue, a man’s glory above all other creatures, which here declares his inward joy. But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott suspects the poet wrote not khabod, glory, but khabed, the liver, or, as with the common use of “bowels,” the heart, the Septuagint’s “tongue” being only a paraphrase; and he takes heart, soul, and flesh together as comprising the whole living man, as in 1 Thess. 5:23.

The last clause carries the weight of the resurrection, and here the readings diverge sharply. Clarke insists there is “no sense in which these and the following words can be spoken of David”: Jesus, even as he breathed out his life, saw that his rest in the grave would be short, long enough to prove his death but not to see corruption, as Peter argues (Acts 2:31). Wesley reads “my flesh shall rest in hope” of the body resting quietly in the grave in confident assurance of its incorruption and its resurrection; the flesh, he grants, is in itself but a dead lump of clay, yet hope is ascribed to it figuratively, as it is to the very creatures (Rom. 8:19).

Ellicott, however, presses the philology: “shall rest in hope” follows the Vulgate, and the Septuagint has “shall tabernacle in hope,” but the true rendering is “shall rest in security”; the psalmist feels that the body must share the immunity from evil which fellowship with God insures, and though the logical issue of this is the doctrine of immortality, “we must not see a conscious reference to it here.” So beneath the shared gladness runs a real divergence: whether the verse is a dying Messiah’s certainty of a swift resurrection, as the Wesleyan voices hear it, or the living confidence of a soul secure in God, into which the hope of immortality is only beginning, faintly, to break.
10:
“For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” — the verse on which Peter and Paul built their argument for the resurrection, and the witnesses work at every word of it. The reformed John Gill first clears away the place of the damned, where Christ never was, his soul being committed to his Father and that day in paradise; “sheol,” like the New Testament “hades,” may rather mean the state of the dead, the invisible world of souls, where the soul of Christ was but was not left; yet Gill judges it “best of all to interpret it of the grave,” taking “my soul” for Christ himself, or for his dead body, laid in the grave but not abandoned there. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that sheol is a pit, a ditch, the grave, or the state of the dead, and that to leave the soul there means to permit the Messiah’s life to continue under the power of death; all men see corruption, being born in sin, but the sinless body of Christ saw none. John Wesley too glosses “hell” as “the state of the dead” and the Holy One as “me thy holy son,” a title peculiar to Christ.

A textual question runs beneath the second line. Clarke observes that “thine Holy One” is plural in the received Hebrew, chasideycha, but singular in the Complutensian Polyglot, in two hundred and sixty-four of Kennicott’s and De Rossi’s manuscripts, and in the quotations of Peter and Paul (Acts 2:27; Acts 13:35), so that the plural is either a corruption or an emphatic singular. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that the received text carries the plural with a marginal note that its plural-sign is superfluous, the weight of manuscripts, versions, and the two apostolic citations all favouring the singular; he would render “Holy One” as “thy chosen” or “beloved One,” the word chasid marking one who stands in covenant favour with Jehovah. On “corruption” he presses further, for the Hebrew shachath is properly a pit, as in Ps. 7:15, so that “to be left to sheol” and “to see the pit” are alike synonyms for “to die”; yet even so, he grants, the verse shows “the first faint scintillation of that light of immortality” whose later dawn justifies the use the New Testament makes of it. So the witnesses divide over the very sense of the dread words — whether “hell” be the grave, the separate state of souls, or (as all deny) the place of the lost, and whether “corruption” name the body’s decay, from which the flesh of Christ was exempt, or simply the pit of death itself.
11:
“Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” — and the psalm closes on the far side of the grave. The reformed John Gill will not read “the path of life” of the way of salvation, which is Christ himself, but of the resurrection of the dead, a passing from death to life shown to Christ not in doctrine but in fact, by his being raised; he was the first to tread that path, the first-fruits and the firstborn from the dead, for though others had been raised before, it was never to an immortal life. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way — “I first shall find the way out of the regions of death, to die no more” — and notes that the Hebrew for life is plural, fitting a resurrection that restores both body and soul; “in thy presence” is literally “thy faces,” the beatific vision (1 John 3:2), and “for evermore” is netzach, an onward and perpetual progression. John Wesley paraphrases throughout of the world to come: “thou wilt raise me from the grave” to everlasting felicity, to the heavenly paradise where God is gloriously present, to the right hand of greatest honour where Christ himself sits (Ps. 110:1), to pleasures that, unlike our transient joys, endure for ever.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the whole as Christ’s recompense for his sufferings: shown the path of life, he could commit his spirit into his Father’s hands, be received into God’s presence, and be set at his right hand in fulness of joy. Yet Henry adds the second application that the others imply, that since Christ is the head of the body, these verses belong also to all Christians animated by his Spirit, who may learn to set the Lord always before them and to put off the body in the hope of a joyful resurrection.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the close more soberly. Removing the Authorized Version’s italics to restore the triplet, he finds in it “another image for the same thought which dominates the psalm — the thought of the happiness of being with God,” the fair heritage, the serene joy, and the enduring pleasure all one; and he sees the larger hope only as a ray faintly triumphing over death itself. So the culminating division stands: where Gill, Clarke, and Wesley find in “the path of life” the very resurrection of Christ that Peter and Paul proclaimed — David’s tomb remaining, the tomb of Christ not — Ellicott hears first the settled peace of a soul that possesses God, upon which the light of immortality has only begun to break.
